about.title: Compton Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Compton is a working city in Los Angeles County, and a steady flow of goods ends up in local homes, garages, and job sites. When something fails — a space heater that ignites, a car seat latch that gives way, a power tool whose guard slips — the person hurt is rarely the one at fault. California handles these cases differently than an ordinary negligence claim. Under strict liability, you generally need to show that the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect and that the defect caused your injury. You do not have to prove the company was careless. Responsibility can also reach beyond the manufacturer to the distributor and the retailer who sold it, whether that was a shop on Compton Boulevard or an online seller shipping to your door. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect Compton residents with an independent attorney who takes product cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: My crash on Rosecrans Avenue happened because a part on my car failed. Is that a product case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It can be both. Compton recorded 333 injury collisions in 2025, and a portion of crashes anywhere involve a component that did not perform as designed, such as a tire, brake system, or airbag. An attorney can look at whether a manufacturer or seller shares responsibility alongside any driver. Keep the vehicle and the failed part exactly as they are until it has been examined.

items.question: What should I do with the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Keep it, and keep everything that came with it — packaging, receipts, instructions, and any warning labels. Do not repair it, return it, or throw it away, because the item itself is often the most important evidence in a strict liability claim. Photograph it and the injury, then write down where and when you bought it.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company did something wrong?
items.answer: Generally, no. Under California's strict liability rules you need to show the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect and that the defect caused your injury. Whether the company meant to cut corners is not usually the question. An independent attorney can explain how those elements apply to your situation.
